title: Practical Skills & Investigation Design
description: Essential biology lab skills — variables, graphing, microscope use, biological drawing, experimental design, and data analysis.

notes.heading: Variables in Scientific Investigations
notes.body: Every well-designed experiment identifies and controls three types of variables: (1) Independent variable (IV) — the factor YOU deliberately change or manipulate. On a graph, this goes on the x-axis (horizontal). Example: if investigating how light intensity affects photosynthesis, light intensity is the IV. (2) Dependent variable (DV) — the factor you MEASURE to see the effect of changing the IV. On a graph, this goes on the y-axis (vertical). Example: the rate of photosynthesis (number of bubbles per minute). (3) Controlled variables (CVs) — all other factors that must be KEPT CONSTANT to ensure a fair test. If these change, you cannot be sure whether the IV or a CV caused any changes in the DV. Example: when varying light intensity, you must control temperature, CO₂ concentration, type of plant, and length of pondweed. Tip: a good investigation changes only ONE variable (the IV) and measures ONE variable (the DV). Everything else is controlled. Common mistake: confusing the IV and DV. Ask yourself — 'What am I changing?' (IV) and 'What am I measuring as a result?' (DV).

notes.heading: Hypotheses and Predictions
notes.body: A hypothesis is a testable, scientific explanation for an observation. It is NOT a guess — it is based on prior knowledge and reasoning. A good hypothesis: (1) States the relationship between the IV and DV. (2) Is specific and measurable. (3) Can be tested and potentially falsified (proven wrong). Format: 'If [change in IV], then [change in DV], because [scientific reasoning].' Example: 'If light intensity increases, then the rate of photosynthesis will increase, because more light energy is available for the light-dependent reactions.' A prediction is the specific outcome you expect if the hypothesis is correct. It should include numbers or a trend direction. A null hypothesis states there will be NO relationship between the variables — this is what statistical tests attempt to disprove. In MYP, you are expected to: state a clear hypothesis with reasoning, design an experiment to test it, and evaluate whether your results support or refute the hypothesis. Remember: data can SUPPORT a hypothesis but never 'prove' it absolutely — future experiments could produce different results.

notes.heading: Using a Light Microscope
notes.body: A light microscope uses visible light and a series of glass lenses to magnify specimens. Parts: Eyepiece lens (usually ×10 magnification) — where you look through. Objective lenses — mounted on the rotating nosepiece; typically ×4 (scanning), ×10 (low power), ×40 (high power). Total magnification = eyepiece magnification × objective magnification (e.g., ×10 × ×40 = ×400). Stage — platform with clips to hold the slide. Coarse focus knob — used ONLY with low-power objectives (big movements, risk of cracking the slide at high power). Fine focus knob — used for precise focusing, especially at high power. Mirror or lamp — directs light through the specimen. Diaphragm — adjusts light intensity. Method: (1) Place the slide on the stage and secure with clips. (2) Start with the lowest power objective (×4). (3) Use the coarse focus to bring the specimen into rough focus. (4) Switch to a higher power objective (×10, then ×40). (5) Use ONLY the fine focus at high power — never the coarse focus. (6) Adjust the diaphragm for optimal contrast. (7) To calculate magnification: magnification = size of image ÷ size of real object. To calculate actual size: actual size = size of image ÷ magnification. Always convert to the same units (mm → µm: multiply by 1000).

notes.heading: Biological Drawing Rules
notes.body: Biological drawings are scientific records, not artwork. Key rules: (1) Use a sharp pencil — never a pen. (2) Draw clean, continuous lines — no sketching, no shading, no colouring. (3) Draw only what you SEE — do not copy textbook diagrams; do not include structures you cannot actually observe. (4) Include a title (underlined) stating what the specimen is, the view (e.g., transverse section, T.S.), and the magnification. (5) Label all visible structures using straight, horizontal ruled lines (use a ruler!). Labels should be to the right of the drawing. (6) No arrows at the ends of label lines. (7) Include a scale bar, not just a magnification number — a scale bar remains accurate if the drawing is resized. (8) Draw the specimen large — it should fill at least half the available space. (9) Indicate the magnification: Mag = size of drawing ÷ size of specimen. (10) Annotate if necessary — brief notes explaining the function of labelled structures can be added. Marks in MYP and DP are awarded for: accuracy, proportion, clear labels, scale, and appropriate detail — not for artistic merit.

notes.heading: Collecting and Recording Data
notes.body: Good data collection is the foundation of reliable science. Guidelines: (1) Use a results table with clear headings including units (e.g., 'Temperature (°C)' not just 'Temperature'). (2) Record data to an appropriate number of decimal places/significant figures — be consistent. (3) Repeat measurements — at least 3 replicates for each condition. (4) Calculate a mean (average) for repeat measurements, excluding anomalous results (outliers). An outlier is a result that does not fit the pattern — it should be identified, excluded from the mean calculation, and its exclusion noted. (5) Qualitative observations (colour changes, appearance) are also data — record them systematically. (6) Identify anomalies and suggest reasons (e.g., measurement error, apparatus malfunction, uncontrolled variable). (7) Calculate the range of repeat measurements (max − min) to assess precision. A small range indicates high precision (repeat measurements are close together). (8) Distinguish between accuracy (how close a measurement is to the true value) and precision (how close repeat measurements are to each other). You can be precise without being accurate (e.g., a poorly calibrated thermometer giving consistently wrong readings).

notes.heading: Graphing and Data Presentation
notes.body: Graphs visualise relationships between variables. Choosing the right graph: Line graph — when both IV and DV are continuous numerical data (e.g., temperature vs. photosynthesis rate). Plot points precisely with small '×' marks, then draw a line or curve of best fit (not dot-to-dot). Bar chart — when the IV is categorical (e.g., comparing different antimicrobials, different mineral deficiencies). Leave gaps between bars. Histogram — when the IV is continuous but grouped into intervals/bins (e.g., frequency of plant heights in ranges: 0-10 cm, 11-20 cm). Bars touch — no gaps. Scatter graph — when investigating correlation between two continuous variables (e.g., height vs. hand span). Plot points; do NOT join them. Add a line of best fit if trend is present. Key rules for ALL graphs: (1) Title describing what the graph shows. (2) Axes labelled with quantity AND units. (3) Sensible scales — use most of the graph paper; do NOT start all axes at zero if it wastes space (but clearly indicate if axes don't start at zero). (4) Independent variable on x-axis; dependent variable on y-axis. (5) Points plotted accurately. (6) Line/curve of best fit — smooth, ignoring anomalous points. It does NOT need to pass through every point, nor through the origin (unless the relationship dictates it should).

notes.heading: Evaluation and Conclusion Writing
notes.body: A strong conclusion in MYP biology: (1) State clearly what your data shows — refer to specific data points or trends from your graph. (2) State whether the results support or refute your hypothesis. Use 'support' not 'prove' — science never absolutely proves anything. (3) Explain the results using scientific knowledge — link back to the biology (e.g., 'Photosynthesis rate increased because light provides energy for the light-dependent reactions'). (4) If results are unexpected, suggest biological reasons — do not just say 'human error'. Evaluation (reflection): (1) Identify sources of error — systematic errors (same error every time, e.g., poorly calibrated equipment — affects accuracy) and random errors (unpredictable variations, e.g., slight timing differences — affects precision). (2) Identify limitations of the method (e.g., 'Counting bubbles is subjective — some were very small'). (3) Suggest realistic, specific improvements (not just 'be more careful' but 'Use a gas syringe to measure oxygen volume precisely instead of counting bubbles'). (4) Suggest extensions — related experiments that would provide further evidence (e.g., 'Investigate the effect of different wavelengths (colours) of light on photosynthesis rate'). (5) Discuss reliability — do your repeats agree? How many replicates did you have? (6) Discuss validity — did you actually measure what you intended to measure? Was it a fair test? Were all controls properly managed?

flashcards.definition: The factor deliberately changed or manipulated by the investigator. Plotted on the x-axis of a graph.
flashcards.example: In 'How does temperature affect enzyme activity?', temperature is the IV.

flashcards.definition: The factor measured to assess the effect of changing the IV. Plotted on the y-axis of a graph.
flashcards.example: In 'How does temperature affect enzyme activity?', the rate of reaction is the DV.

flashcards.definition: A factor that is kept constant throughout an investigation to ensure it is a fair test — only the IV should affect the DV.
flashcards.example: When investigating light and photosynthesis, you must control: temperature, CO₂ concentration, type/length of pondweed, and water volume.

flashcards.definition: A testable, scientific explanation predicting the relationship between the IV and DV, based on prior knowledge and reasoning.
flashcards.example: 'If light intensity increases, then the rate of photosynthesis will increase, because more light energy drives the light-dependent reactions.'

flashcards.definition: Eyepiece lens magnification × objective lens magnification. ×10 eyepiece with ×40 objective = ×400 total magnification.
flashcards.example: At ×400, a human cheek cell appears roughly the size of a small coin.

flashcards.definition: A line of known length added to a biological drawing or micrograph, representing a specific actual size. Remains accurate when the image is resized.
flashcards.example: A scale bar labelled '50 µm' means that line represents 50 micrometres in the real specimen.

flashcards.definition: A data point that does not fit the pattern of the rest of the data. Should be identified, excluded from mean calculations, and explained.
flashcards.example: Five readings: 10, 11, 9, 32, 10. The value 32 is anomalous — likely a measurement or recording error.

flashcards.definition: Accuracy = how close a measurement is to the TRUE value. Precision = how close REPEAT measurements are to each other (represented by small range/standard deviation).
flashcards.example: A scale that consistently reads '52 kg' for a 50 kg person is precise (consistent) but NOT accurate (off by 2 kg).

flashcards.definition: A smooth line or curve drawn through data points on a graph showing the overall trend. Does NOT need to pass through every point; ignores outliers.
flashcards.example: Do NOT play 'dot-to-dot' — a line of best fit smooths out random errors in individual data points.

flashcards.definition: An error that affects ALL measurements in the same way (e.g., poorly calibrated equipment). Affects accuracy, not precision.
flashcards.example: A thermometer reading 3°C too high will make all temperature measurements 3°C too high — results are precise but inaccurate.

flashcards.definition: Unpredictable variations in measurements caused by limitations of equipment or human judgement. Affects precision; can be reduced by taking repeat readings and averaging.
flashcards.example: Timing with a stopwatch — reaction time varies slightly each attempt. Multiple repeats and calculating a mean reduces the impact.

flashcards.definition: An investigation where only the independent variable is changed; all other variables (controlled variables) are kept constant. Ensures valid conclusions about cause and effect.
flashcards.example: Comparing plant growth with different fertilisers — must control water, light, temperature, soil type, pot size, and starting plant size.

questions.stem: A student investigates how temperature affects the rate of enzyme activity. What is the independent variable?
choices: The rate of enzyme activity
Temperature
The type of enzyme used
The volume of the reaction mixture
questions.explanation: The independent variable is what the student deliberately changes — in this case, the temperature. The rate of enzyme activity is the dependent variable (what is being measured).

questions.stem: A microscope has a ×10 eyepiece and a ×40 objective lens. What is the total magnification?
Why should you NEVER use the coarse focus knob when using a high-power (×40) objective lens?
choices: The coarse focus knob does not work at high power
The lens is too close to the slide — using the coarse focus could drive the lens into and crack the slide
The coarse focus knob is only for the eyepiece
High-power objectives do not need focusing
questions.explanation: At high power, the objective lens is very close to the slide (working distance of ~0.5 mm). The coarse focus knob moves the stage large distances — it is easy to crash the lens into the slide, breaking both.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a GOOD hypothesis for a biology experiment?
choices: I think temperature will affect enzymes
'If temperature increases (up to 40°C), then the rate of starch breakdown by amylase will increase, because enzymes have more kinetic energy and collisions with substrate occur more frequently'
Temperature and enzymes are related
I predict the enzyme will work faster because my textbook says so
questions.explanation: A good hypothesis includes the relationship between IV and DV, AND a scientific explanation (reasoning). The first and third options are too vague. Textbooks provide evidence, not hypotheses.

questions.stem: A student's biological drawing of a cell is 50 mm across. The actual cell is 0.05 mm. What is the drawing's magnification?
questions.explanation: Magnification = image size ÷ actual size = 50 ÷ 0.05 = ×1000. Both measurements must be in the same units.

questions.stem: A student draws a plant cell and labels it with pen, adds shaded areas, and sketches arrows. Why would this lose marks?
choices: Biological drawings should be in pencil with clean lines, no shading/colouring, and labels on straight ruled lines — not arrows
The drawing is not artistic enough
Plant cells should be drawn in colour
Drawings are never used in biology
questions.explanation: Biological drawing conventions require: pencil only, clear continuous lines, no shading/colouring/sketching, and horizontal ruled label lines (no arrows). These rules ensure drawings are clear, reproducible scientific records.

questions.stem: Five measurements of a plant's height over 2 weeks: 10 cm, 12 cm, 11 cm, 35 cm, 10 cm. What is the most appropriate way to handle the anomalous result?
choices: Ignore it silently and calculate the mean of the remaining four values
Identify 35 cm as anomalous, exclude it from the mean calculation, note its exclusion, and suggest a reason (e.g., measurement or recording error)
Include it — all data must be used regardless
Change 35 cm to 13 cm to fit the pattern
questions.explanation: An anomalous result should be transparently identified, excluded from the mean, and the exclusion should be explained with a plausible reason. Never alter data to fit expectations — this is scientific fraud.

questions.stem: What type of graph is most appropriate for data on the number of students with each blood type (A, B, AB, O)?
choices: Line graph
Scatter graph
Bar chart
Histogram
questions.explanation: Blood type is categorical data. Bar charts (with gaps between bars) display categorical independent variables. Line graphs are for continuous data; histograms are for grouped continuous data.

questions.stem: Why is it important to include a scale bar rather than just a magnification number on a biological drawing?
choices: Scale bars look more professional
A scale bar remains accurate if the image is enlarged or reduced (photocopied, projected); a magnification number becomes incorrect if the image size changes
Magnification numbers are difficult to calculate
Scale bars are easier to draw
questions.explanation: If a drawing labelled '×400' is photocopied at 200%, the actual magnification is now ×800 — the label is wrong. A scale bar represents an actual length and scales proportionally with the image, remaining accurate.

questions.stem: A student's conclusion states: 'My results prove my hypothesis was correct.' What is the issue with this statement?
choices: Results support or refute a hypothesis; they never 'prove' it — future experiments could produce different results or alternative explanations
Hypotheses are never correct
The student should not have a hypothesis
Only professional scientists can draw conclusions
questions.explanation: Science is provisional — conclusions are always open to revision with new evidence. Use 'support' not 'prove'. One experiment provides evidence, not absolute proof.

questions.stem: A balance consistently reads 2.3 g too low for every measurement. This is an example of:
choices: Random error — it varies unpredictably
Systematic error — a consistent bias in all measurements affecting accuracy
Human error — the student is reading incorrectly
No error — balances are always perfectly accurate
questions.explanation: A systematic error affects all measurements equally in one direction. The measurements may be precise (consistent) but they are inaccurate (offset from the true value). Recalibrating the balance would fix this.

questions.stem: When is a line graph more appropriate than a bar chart?
choices: When the independent variable is continuous numerical data (e.g., temperature, concentration, time)
When the independent variable is categorical (e.g., type of disinfectant)
When you have fewer than 5 data points
Line graphs are always better
questions.explanation: Line graphs show trends and relationships between two continuous numerical variables. Bar charts are for categorical or discrete independent variables with no intermediate values between categories.

questions.stem: In an investigation, a student measures the effect of light intensity on photosynthesis rate. Which variable MUST be controlled?
choices: Light intensity — that is what is being changed
Oxygen production — that is what is being measured
Temperature — it also affects photosynthesis, so if it changes, you cannot tell whether light or temperature caused the effect
The number of bubbles counted
questions.explanation: Temperature affects the rate of photosynthesis independently of light. If temperature fluctuates, you cannot attribute changes in the DV solely to your IV. All other factors that could affect the DV must be controlled.

questions.stem: A student finds a 'line of best fit' that does not pass through the origin (0,0) even though 0 light intensity means 0 photosynthesis. What should they do?
choices: Force the line through the origin to make it look correct
Draw the line where the data points suggest it should go, and evaluate why the data may show a non-zero intercept — consider systematic errors or experimental limitations
Ignore the discrepancy — the origin does not matter
Remove the data points near the origin
questions.explanation: A line of best fit should follow the actual data, not preconceived expectations. If it does not pass through the origin where theory predicts it should, this is a finding to discuss in the evaluation — not something to hide or force.

questions.stem: Why are 3 repeat measurements better than a single measurement?
choices: More data impresses the teacher
Repeats allow you to calculate a mean, identify anomalous results, and assess precision (via range) — increasing reliability of conclusions
Three is a magic number in biology
Repeats eliminate all sources of error
questions.explanation: Repeats enable you to (1) calculate a more representative mean, (2) spot outliers, and (3) assess how consistent your measurements are (small range = high precision). They increase the reliability of your findings.
